title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
statement:
Return `true` when `nums` could have been produced by taking some array sorted in non-decreasing order (repeated values allowed) and rotating it by some number of positions `x` (zero is allowed), and `false` otherwise.

Rotating an array `A` of length `n` by `x` positions gives the array `B` with `B[i] = A[(i + x) % n]` for every index `i`; in other words, the first `x` elements are moved, in order, to the back.
notes:
## Intuition

The hint suggests trying every rotation and comparing against the sorted array, which is O(n²). There is a simpler test. Read `nums` as a circle (the last element is followed by the first). A sorted array read this way goes up or stays level everywhere except at most once, where it wraps from its largest value back to its smallest. Rotating does not change the circle, so `nums` is valid exactly when the circle has at most one place where a value is followed by a smaller one.

## Approach

1. Set `drops = 0`.
2. For each index `i`, look at its circular neighbour `next = nums[(i + 1) % n]`.
3. If `nums[i] > next`, count a drop.
4. As soon as `drops` exceeds 1, return `false`.
5. If the loop finishes, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`, `n = 5`. Pairs: 3→4, 4→5 go up; 5→1 is a drop (`drops = 1`); 1→2 goes up; the wrap pair 2→3 goes up. Only one drop, so the answer is `true`.

For Example 2, `[2, 1, 3, 4]` has a drop at 2→1 and another at the wrap 4→2, so it returns `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the circle.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Include the wrap-around pair (last, first); without it `[2, 1, 3, 4]` looks valid.
- Equal neighbours are not drops, since duplicates are allowed in a non-decreasing array.
- A single element or an array of equal values has no drops and is valid.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `drops` | how many circular neighbours go from a larger to a smaller value |
| `i` | current index |
| `next` | the element after `nums[i]` on the circle |

narration.2: Remember the length so the neighbour index can wrap around.
narration.3: Count the places where the sequence goes down.
narration.4: Visit every element once, including the last one, whose neighbour is the first.
narration.5: Take the next element on the circle; the modulo wraps the last index back to 0.
narration.6: A larger value followed by a smaller one is a drop.
narration.9: A rotated sorted array has at most one drop, the wrap from its maximum to its minimum.
narration.10: Two drops prove nums cannot be a rotated sorted array.
narration.13: At most one drop: cutting the circle right after it gives a sorted array.
